title: Valid Parentheses
statement:
You are given a string `s` made only of the six characters `(`, `)`, `[`, `]`, `{` and `}`.

Return `true` if the brackets are **balanced**: every opening bracket is closed by a bracket of the same type, brackets close in the reverse order they were opened (so `([)]` is not balanced), and no closing bracket appears without a matching opener before it.

The empty string counts as balanced.
hints: When you reach a closing bracket, which earlier opening bracket must it match? Is it the first one, or the most recent one still waiting?
The bracket that must close next is always the most recently opened unclosed one — last in, first out. Keep the unclosed openers on a stack.
Scan left to right. Push every opener. On a closer, fail if the stack is empty or its top is the wrong type; otherwise pop. At the end the string is balanced only if the stack is empty.
followups: If the string only contained one bracket type, can you do it in O(1) extra space?
How would you return the minimum number of insertions needed to make it balanced?
How would you find the length of the longest balanced substring?
explain: Walk the string once with a stack of opening brackets. An opener is pushed. A closer must match the opener on top of the stack — if the stack is empty or the types differ, return false; otherwise pop. After the scan, any openers left on the stack were never closed, so the answer is stack.isEmpty(). Each character is pushed and popped at most once: O(n) time, O(n) space in the worst case (all openers). In Java use ArrayDeque<Character> rather than the legacy synchronized Stack class; an odd length is an easy early exit. The tempting alternative — repeatedly deleting "()", "[]" and "{}" until nothing changes — is O(n^2) on deeply nested input.
